extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, discourse analysts, and linguists studying news production and news values
extracted.subtask_description: Apply and evaluate theoretical lists of news values (especially Galtung & Ruge's twelve factors) to front-page newspaper stories to determine which criteria drive news selection in a specific national context (Iran). Includes a methodological checklist for identifying news values in articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency (F1)
rubrics_metrics.description: An event that unfolds within a publication cycle of the news medium is more likely to be selected than one that takes place over a long period of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors treat frequency as a complementary prerequisite: recency is necessary but not sufficient. In the Iranian corpus frequency alone did not select items; online editions reduce the prominence of F1 by covering very recent events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold (F2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events have to pass a threshold before being recorded at all; the greater the intensity (the more gruesome the murder or the more casualties in an accident), the greater the impact and the more likely it is to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study few stories exhibited a considerable threshold; when present, indefinite pronouns and quantifiers (many, most) sometimes signal magnitude rather than a discrete high threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguity (F3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more clearly an event can be understood and interpreted without multiple meanings, the more likely it is to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that 'unambiguity' is itself ambiguous: it often refers to composition/style rather than the event. It may be a general prerequisite of writing level; sometimes ambiguity can be valued, so its role as an independent news value is questionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningfulness (F4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The culturally familiar is more likely to be selected (meaningfulness to audiences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningfulness was highly frequent in the corpus, especially in foreign news about culturally proximate countries; it helps explain why geographically distant but culturally close events are selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consonance (F5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The news selector may be able to predict (due to experience) events that will be newsworthy, thus forming a 'pre-image' of an event, which in turn increases its chances of becoming news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consonance (also called cultural resonance, pre-fabrication, predictability) was the second most frequent factor in Iran. It often collocated with reference to elite people; includes geographical and cultural proximity (e.g., Syria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpectedness (F6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among events meaningful and/or consonant, the unexpected or rare event is more likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpectedness (also labeled Surprise, The Unusual, Oddity) is a general characteristic but was not centrally important in the Iranian sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity / Follow-up (F7)
rubrics_metrics.description: An event already in the news has a good chance of remaining in the news because it has become familiar and easier to interpret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity (Follow-up/Co-option) played a minor role in this study; when broadened to competition with other media, its impact became more considerable in the Iranian context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition (F8)
rubrics_metrics.description: An event may be included as news less because of its intrinsic news value than because it fits into the overall composition or balance of a newspaper or news broadcast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficult to judge from front pages; authors found composition/balance not a major determinant for front-page selection in most cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite nations (F9)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actions of elite nations are seen as more consequential than the actions of other nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the Iranian corpus reference to EU, USA, neighbouring and culturally close countries, and international organizations (UN, IAEA) was relatively important for foreign news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to elite people (F10)
rubrics_metrics.description: The actions of elite people, likely to be famous, may be seen by news selectors as having more consequence than others; news audiences may identify with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Found to be the single most frequent news value in Iranian newspapers (mostly politicians). The paper notes ambiguity in 'elite' (rock star vs Nobel laureate), and links to constructs like celebrity, power elite; government-funded press may skew coverage toward politicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to persons / Personalization (F11)
rubrics_metrics.description: News that can be presented in terms of individual people rather than abstractions is likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although many items had human actors, themes were often abstract (e.g., geopolitical disputes), so personalization was not a strongly significant factor in this corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to something negative / Bad news (F12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad events are generally unambiguous and newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a small proportion (<6%) of studied items had an explicitly negative theme; many political quarrels were coded under consonance rather than F12.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Power elite
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of a revised list of contemporary news values emphasizing power elite as a driver of newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harcup & O'Neill (2001) recast Galtung & Ruge for modern press; authors cite Power elite as one of the updated values to consider alongside others like celebrity and follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fame or celebrity status increases newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a modern iteration of elite-person coverage; appears across comparative news-values lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment value makes a story more newsworthy for audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of Harcup & O'Neill's updated list; represents non-political/popular-culture drivers of selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected or surprising events increase a story's newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maps to Galtung & Ruge's unexpectedness but re-emphasized in updated lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Bad news (recast)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that report negative outcomes or threats are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reiterates the salience of negative events in modern lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Good news
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive stories (good news) are recognized as a distinct category of news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that positive outcomes also have audience appeal and can be selected for editorial reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Scale or numbers (magnitude) increase the newsworthiness of an event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely related to Threshold but emphasizing quantifiable impact; the authors' checklist explicitly asks about numbers and scales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevance to the audience's lives increases the chance of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlaps with Meaningfulness and Consonance; in the Iranian study relevance often hinges on cultural proximity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Ongoing coverage and sequence of stories increase continued newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equates to Continuity; authors found limited pure follow-up effect unless competition with other media was considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harcup & O'Neill revised criteria: Media agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that fit the media's agenda or priorities are more likely to be selected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflects institutional and editorial priorities; relates to composition and consonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's formal news values: Linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the story linked, or capable of being linked, with a prior event, happening, occurrence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Linkage helps situate stories within ongoing narratives; Hall contrasts formal values like linkage with deeper ideological values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's formal news values: Recency
rubrics_metrics.description: Has it happened recently?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recency overlaps with Frequency; Hall uses it as a formal criterion before moving to ideological analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's formal news values: Newsworthiness of event/person
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the event or person meet an a priori sense of newsworthiness?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hall notes this criterion can beg questions; it's used as a surface-level/formal determinant before ideological factors are considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hall's ideological news values (consensus knowledge / deep structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hidden 'deep structure' or consensus knowledge provides an ideological framework that shapes what is foregrounded as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts formal values; ideological values explain why certain events are framed and which interpretations are preferred; central to CDA approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: MacShane categories: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict as a type/category of newsworthy events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MacShane's taxonomy (1979) lists conflict as a primary attractor of news attention; conflict often maps to political/power themes in the Iranian corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: MacShane categories: Hardship and danger to the community
rubrics_metrics.description: Events involving community hardship or danger are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of alternative taxonomies emphasizing social impact and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: MacShane categories: Unusualness
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are unusual or rare are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maps to Unexpectedness; used in earlier lists of news categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: MacShane categories: Scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Scandal generates newsworthiness due to moral breach or salacious detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scandal often overlaps with personalization and elite-person coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: MacShane categories: Individualism
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories emphasizing individuals and individual actions are newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to personalization (F11) and human-interest framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology / metalingual social factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideology, competition, and relations of power (metalingual elements) that shape selection and framing of news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors argue these factors are central yet underrepresented in Galtung & Ruge's list; in Iran ideology and power relations play a considerable role in gatekeeping and should be treated as explicit selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist for recognizing main news values (methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set of operational questions used to identify the primary news value(s) of an item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist items used in this study: What is/are the main news value(s) of the title? Is the news domestic or foreign, and if foreign which element makes it interesting for Iranian audiences? Who are the main actors — can they be considered elites? Is the news centered on an interview and who is referenced? Does the story have follow-ups or refer to previous events? Is there reference to numbers/scales and are they presented as significant? Is the theme positive or negative? The authors note in ambiguous cases they used intuition and background knowledge; multiple values per story are possible and order is irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level separation of news factors (pre-production/production/post-production)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish technical/exclusive news factors across stages: pre-production (choosing event), production (news composition), and post-production (publication/broadcasting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors recommend future studies separate levels to improve theoretical precision; some factors operate at selection time, others at composition or dissemination, and recognizing this can clarify which criteria govern each stage.
